parsed.explanation: The counterexample checks out. With F_i = {c, a_i, b_1,...,b_{i-1}} (all containing c, hence pairwise intersecting, with finite member F_1 = {c,a_1}), each B_n = {a_1,...,a_n,b_n} is a transversal (it meets F_i via a_i for i<=n and via b_n for i>n) and is minimal (dropping a_j misses F_j; dropping b_n misses F_{n+1}). So infinitely many minimal finite transversals exist and the "finite blocker fact" is false; the alleged Koenig/pruning proof must therefore fail. This is exactly the ledger's warning that pairwise intersection alone gives no finiteness. The write-up derives its entire finiteness (B_1,...,B_s, hence L and T) from this false lemma and never uses the arithmetic large-prime erasure (no term-minimality/size argument appears anywhere), so L6.2 is unestablished.
